what_its_for: Eteplirsen is used to treat Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) in patients who have a specific change (mutation) in the dystrophin gene that can be treated by skipping exon 51. DMD is a genetic disease that causes muscles to weaken and break down over time. This medicine helps your body make a shorter but partially working form of a protein called dystrophin, which muscles need to stay healthy.
how_to_take: Eteplirsen is given as an infusion (a slow injection) directly into a vein (IV). It is not a pill or liquid you take by mouth. A trained healthcare provider, such as a nurse or doctor, will give you this medicine in a clinic, hospital, or sometimes at home. Each infusion takes about 35 to 60 minutes. You will receive this treatment once every week, on the same day each week if possible.
dosing: The usual dose is 30 mg for every kilogram (kg) of your body weight, given once a week by IV infusion. Your doctor will calculate the exact dose based on your weight. Do not try to change your dose on your own. Always follow your doctor's instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss a scheduled infusion, contact your doctor or healthcare team right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Try to get back on your regular weekly schedule. Do not try to give yourself a double dose to make up for a missed one.
storage: Eteplirsen is stored and prepared by a healthcare professional or specialty pharmacy, so you may not need to store it at home. If you do keep it at home, store unopened vials in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do not freeze it. Keep it in the original box to protect it from light. Once the medicine is mixed (diluted) and ready to use, it should be used within 4 hours if kept at room temperature, or within 24 hours if kept in the refrigerator. Keep all medicines out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: There are no specific foods, drinks, or activities you must completely avoid while taking eteplirsen. However, always tell your doctor and pharmacist about ALL other medicines you take, including vitamins, supplements, and herbal products, so they can check for any possible interactions. Follow your healthcare team's general advice about staying as active and healthy as possible with your condition.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get medical help right away if you notice any of the following during or after your infusion: redness, swelling, pain, or a rash at the infusion site; fever or chills; nausea or vomiting; flushing (feeling warm or red in the face); dizziness or feeling faint; trouble breathing; chest tightness; swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat; or any new or worsening symptoms. Also call your doctor if you have any concerns about your treatment or if your condition seems to be getting worse.
when_it_works: Eteplirsen may start helping your body make dystrophin protein within weeks, but it can take many months before you or your doctor notice any changes in muscle strength or function. Some patients may see very small or gradual improvements. This medicine is not a cure for DMD, but it is meant to slow the progression of the disease. Be patient and keep all of your scheduled appointments so your doctor can monitor how well the medicine is working for you.
special_populations: Children: Eteplirsen has been studied in children with DMD and is approved for use in patients of all ages who have the specific exon 51 mutation. Doses are based on body weight. Older adults: DMD mainly affects children and young males, so there is limited information about use in older adults. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have any kidney or liver problems, as this may affect how your body processes the medicine. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: It is not known if eteplirsen is safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
